summary: A response to RFC 1550 submitted to the IETF IPng area by the Electric Power Research Institute, giving its comments on IPng. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo gives the Electric Power Research Institute's view of what IPng should support. It emphasizes industrial applications, scalable addressing, routing, transition, and coordination with established standards.

questions: what requirements did epri give for ipng
subtitle: The Electric Power Research Institute's comments on IPng requirements.

tldr.problem: EPRI wanted IPng planning to address large-scale industrial communications needs and align with existing standards and investments.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements for address scalability, routing efficiency, support for existing applications, transition, administration, mobility, and additional convergent standards.
tldr.outcome: It submits EPRI's perspective to the IPng area and says publication does not imply acceptance of its ideas.

today: RFC 1673 is Informational and records the Electric Power Research Institute's comments on IPng. It does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: EPRI's IPng Perspective
sections.content:
The Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) submitted these comments in response to the IPng white-paper solicitation. The memo says the electric power industry was a heavy user of the Internet Protocol Suite while also following a long-term strategy based on international and national standards.

EPRI describes its Utility Communications Architecture and Database Access Integrated Services specifications as based on the OSI model and international standards. It argues that IPng planning should address the needs of public and private sectors from national and international perspectives.
sections.plainLanguage: EPRI presents the requirements it sees from the electric power industry's perspective. The memo describes both its use of Internet protocols and its preference for formal standards work.

sections.title: Scale, Routing, and Existing Applications
sections.content:
The memo calls for IPng to support industrial OSI applications with high integrity and says the address space should overcome the limitations of 32-bit formats; it considers a format of 20 octets or more suitable. It also calls for economy in routing databases as networks grow and support for existing Internet and OSI applications.

Its engineering considerations include route aggregation, service selection, low-frequency host advertisements, policy-based administration, flexible configuration, and dynamic addressing. It also asks that addressing support other schemes such as X.121 and E.164 and preserve Internet domain names.
sections.plainLanguage: EPRI wants IPng to scale beyond 32-bit formats, keep routing information manageable, and support existing applications and other address schemes.

sections.title: Transition and Operational Flexibility
sections.content:
EPRI calls for a solution based on mature, internationally agreed standards and available implementations. It proposes an evolutionary transition using OSI, and a dual-network-layer strategy that would avoid changes to existing inter-domain routing protocols while supporting protocols such as IPX and AppleTalk.

The memo also asks for flexible address allocation, simplified configuration, support for multi-homed hosts and applications, and mobility through dynamic addressing with little human intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal emphasizes a gradual transition and configuration that can adapt to different organizations and technologies. It also calls for hosts to learn addresses with little manual work.

sections.title: Status of the Comments
sections.content: RFC 1673 is an informational submission to the IETF IPng area. It states that publication does not imply acceptance of any ideas in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC records EPRI's input for IPng discussions. Its publication does not mean the IPng area accepted the proposals.

references.text: Rose, M. and D. Cass, "ISO Transport Service on Top of the TCP", RFC 1006, May 1987.
Gross, P., ed., "IP: Next Generation (IPng) White Paper Solicitation", RFC 1550, December 1993.
